turns.output: For as long as I can remember, the unmistakable aroma of garlic sizzling in oil, followed by the sharp, comforting tang of vinegar and soy sauce, meant one thing: Lola was making chicken adobo. In our family, this dish is far more than just a staple weeknight meal; it is the heartbeat of our kitchen and a savory link to our heritage. For generations, the recipe lived only in memory, measured by instinct, a splash of this, and a handful of that. Every Sunday, its rich, mahogany glaze and succulent, tender chicken brought us crowding around the dining table, with bowls of steaming white rice ready to soak up every last drop of garlicky sauce. Today, I am finally putting pen to paper to share our cherished family version. Whether you are cooking for a crowd or simply craving a taste of home, may this adobo bring warmth to yours.

Every family has a dish that immediately feels like home, and in ours, that dish is chicken adobo. Passed down through three generations, this beloved Filipino classic has anchored our Sunday dinners and special celebrations for decades. The magic lies in its humble yet deeply comforting ingredients. Tender chicken thighs simmer slowly in a savory bath of soy sauce, tangy cane vinegar, crushed garlic, whole black peppercorns, and fragrant bay leaves. As the pot bubbles gently on the stove, the rich aroma fills the entire kitchen, drawing everyone to the table before dinner is even served. While every household puts its own unique spin on this timeless stew, our family version strikes the perfect balance between salty, sour, and slightly sweet. Served over a steaming mound of fluffy white rice to soak up every last drop of glossy sauce, this recipe brings warmth, history, and pure joy to every bite.

Have you ever noticed how a rainbow appears after a storm? That’s because sunlight isn’t actually white—it’s a mix of every color of the rainbow traveling together! 

Each color of light moves in waves, kind of like ripples in a pond. Red light has long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light have super short, choppy waves. 

When sunlight reaches Earth, it has to travel through our atmosphere, which is packed with billions of tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Most of the long waves—like red, orange, and yellow—zoom right past these molecules without bumping into them. 

Blue light, however, has short, energetic waves that are just the right size to slam straight into those gas molecules. When that happens, the blue light bounces off and scatters in every direction. When you look up, you’re seeing all that scattered blue light bouncing around above you!

Wait—if violet has even shorter waves than blue, why isn't the sky purple? Two reasons: the sun actually sends out more blue light than violet, and human eyes are simply much better at seeing blue. Plus, at sunset, sunlight travels through way more air to reach you, scattering the blue away before it arrives and leaving the reds and oranges behind!

Have you ever wondered why the sky turns such a brilliant shade of blue on a sunny day? It all comes down to how sunlight travels and bumps into Earth's atmosphere.

Even though sunlight looks white, it is actually made up of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. Each color travels in a wave, and every wave has a different size. Red and orange light travel in long, lazy waves. Blue and violet light travel in much shorter, choppier waves.

When sunlight reaches Earth, it enters our atmosphere, which is packed with billions of tiny, invisible gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. Because red and yellow waves are so long, they glide right past these tiny molecules without much trouble. However, the short, choppy blue waves crash right into the gas molecules and scatter in every direction across the sky. Scientists call this Rayleigh scattering. When you look up, you are seeing all that scattered blue light bouncing down to your eyes.

Wait, if violet waves are even shorter than blue ones, why isn't the sky purple? First, the sun gives off more blue light than violet. Second, human eyes are simply much better at detecting blue!

Imagine cooking a meal. Instead of driving to the grocery store every time you need salt, you keep a jar in your pantry. A **browser cache** works the exact same way for the internet.

When you visit a website for the first time, your browser (like Chrome or Safari) downloads all the pieces that make up the page—text, images, logos, and styling—from a distant computer called a server. Downloading these pieces takes a little time.

To make future visits faster, your browser saves copies of these files directly on your device in a temporary storage area called the **cache**.

The next time you visit that website, your browser checks its cache first. Instead of downloading the site’s logo or background images over the internet again, it simply grabs the saved copies straight from your device. Because loading from your own device is much quicker than downloading from the internet, the page opens much faster and uses less data.

Of course, websites get updated. To keep you from seeing old versions, cached files have expiration dates. When a file expires, your browser checks back with the server to download fresh updates, keeping your browsing both fast and current.

Imagine going to the grocery store every single time you want a glass of milk, instead of keeping a carton in your fridge. That is what browsing the internet would be like without a browser cache.

A browser cache is a temporary storage space on your computer or phone. When you visit a website for the first time, your web browser downloads everything needed to display that page, such as text, images, logos, and layout styles. Instead of deleting those files when you leave, your browser saves copies of them in the cache.

The next time you visit that same website, your browser checks its cache first. Because it already has the images and design files saved locally on your device, it loads them immediately from your storage rather than downloading them over the internet again. This makes pages load much faster and uses less data.

Of course, websites change over time. To prevent you from seeing outdated content, website owners attach expiration rules to their files. When a saved file expires, your browser automatically asks the website for a fresh copy. You can also clear your cache manually whenever you want to force your browser to download everything anew.

Starting to code at forty is not a disadvantage; it is your secret weapon. Forget the stereotype of the teenage prodigy in a hoodie. Real software engineering is not about typing fast. The Atlantic did not give things back without a reason, and it certainly didn't make them ring.

Julian paused halfway down the slick basalt steps, lantern swaying in his weathered hand. Above the hiss of receding foam and the rhythmic groan of the lighthouse's brass gears, a sharp, bright chime cut through the salted air. It was an absurdly cheerful sound, synthetic and alien against the grey sprawl of the breakwater.

He followed it down to the tide pools, his boots crunching on barnacles. There, wedged in a jagged cleft where the surf boiled white, lay a black slab of glass. Its screen pulsed with a ghostly blue light, illuminating the wet kelp curled around it like clutching fingers.

*Unknown Caller.*

Julian knelt, the spray soaking through his oilskins. The nearest mainland town was twelve miles across a churning channel, and no vessel had braved the shoals since Tuesday’s gale. Yet the phone sat dry in its hollow, untouched by the rising tide, buzzing insistently against the stone.

The screen dimmed, then flared again. A second call. Holding his breath against the wind, Julian reached out, wiped the mist from the glass, and slid his thumb across the answer bar.

The gale had finally broken before dawn, leaving the headland slick with black kelp and scattered driftwood. Thomas pulled his oilskin tighter around his shoulders and picked his way down the wet granite steps toward the tide line. After forty years of tending the beacon, he knew the storm’s habits. It always gave something back in the morning, usually tangled nets, splintered crates, or drowned gulls.

He paused near a jagged shelf of basalt where the white foam still hissed. Beneath the rhythmic boom of the Atlantic, another sound cut through the salt air. It was sharp, melodic, and entirely wrong for this lonely edge of the world.

Thomas squinted into a shallow crevice flooded with dark water. Partly buried in a bed of crushed mussels lay a small glass rectangle. Its screen burned bright blue against the gray stone, casting a pale glow over the barnacles. A cheerful chime echoed from the wet speaker, insistent and alien.

No ship had wrecked on the reef last night. The radar had stayed clear until sunrise. Slowly, Thomas knelt on the cold rock, his stiff fingers hovering over the vibrating glass, wondering who could possibly be calling the end of the earth.

I just wrapped up my first year as an engineering manager. It’s been the most challenging—and rewarding—year of my career.

Moving from writing code to leading people requires a complete mindset shift. Here are three lessons that stuck with me:

1. Stop trying to have all the answers. Your job isn't to be the top technical problem-solver anymore. It’s to ask the right questions and create space for your team to shine.

2. Embrace uncomfortable conversations. Avoiding tough feedback only hurts everyone in the long run. Clarity is kindness, even when it feels awkward in the moment.

3. Redefine productivity. As an engineer, you measure days in merged PRs. As a manager, your impact shows up in unblocked teammates and long-term growth. Learning to trust that slower feedback loop takes patience.

Still learning every day. To fellow managers: what surprised you most in year one?

#EngineeringManagement #TechLeadership #CareerGrowth

One year ago, I transitioned from writing code to managing engineers. The learning curve was steep, and I made plenty of mistakes. Here are three lessons that defined my first year:

1. Redefine your productivity. Seeing an empty commit graph initially made me anxious. I had to learn that unblocking a teammate or clarifying a roadmap creates far more impact than shipping code myself.

2. Resist the urge to rescue. My instinct was to jump in and fix technical hurdles. Stepping back gave my team space to grow, take ownership, and find better solutions than I would have.

3. Listen more than you speak. Real insights rarely appear in status meetings. They surface during candid 1:1 conversations where people feel safe sharing what is actually slowing them down.

Management is a completely different craft, and I am still learning every day. To fellow managers, what surprised you most in your first year?

Set in the Jazz Age of 1922 New York, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s *The Great Gatsby* follows Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman who rents a cottage next to the lavish mansion of the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. Nick soon learns that Gatsby’s extravagant parties are merely an attempt to attract the attention of Nick’s cousin, Daisy Buchanan, whom Gatsby loved years earlier before leaving for World War I. Though Daisy is now married to the arrogant, unfaithful Tom Buchanan, Gatsby convinces Nick to reunite them. An affair ensues, culminating in a tense confrontation in Manhattan. On the drive home, Daisy, behind the wheel of Gatsby’s car, accidentally strikes and kills Tom’s mistress, Myrtle Wilson. Gatsby takes the blame to protect Daisy, leading Myrtle’s grieving husband to fatally shoot Gatsby before taking his own life. Disillusioned when Daisy and Tom flee without attending Gatsby’s funeral, Nick decides to return to the Midwest.

Beneath its glittering surface, the novel explores the hollowness and corruption of the American Dream, showing how the relentless pursuit of wealth often breeds moral decay. It critiques rigid class divisions between "old" and "new" money while examining the tragedy of Gatsby’s nostalgia—his fatal belief that the past can be recaptured.

Johannes Gutenberg’s invention of the movable-type printing press in the mid-15th century transformed Europe by democratizing knowledge. Previously, books were painstakingly copied by hand, making them rare, expensive, and largely confined to the clergy and wealthy elite. Printing drastically reduced production costs and time, triggering an unprecedented explosion of accessible information.

This surge in affordable texts fueled rising literacy across social classes. Printers increasingly published in vernacular languages rather than solely in Latin, which helped standardize national languages and foster shared cultural identities. Ideas that once took decades to travel could now reach thousands within weeks.

Consequently, the printing press became the engine of Europe’s greatest cultural shifts. It fueled the Protestant Reformation by rapidly spreading Martin Luther’s writings and vernacular Bibles, breaking the Catholic Church’s monopoly on religious interpretation. It also accelerated the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution. Scholars could now compare identical texts, verify data, and build upon discoveries accurately without the transcription errors of hand-copied manuscripts. By dismantling institutional gatekeeping and creating an interconnected intellectual public, the printing press revolutionized communication, empowered individual inquiry, and laid the groundwork for the modern world.

This surge in available texts fueled a rapid rise in literacy across the continent. Printers increasingly produced works in vernacular languages, such as German, French, and English, rather than exclusively in Latin. This shift fostered shared national identities and allowed ordinary people to engage directly with new ideas.

Politically and religiously, the press decentralized authority. During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther’s critiques of the Catholic Church spread across Europe within weeks, sparking widespread debate and fracturing religious unity. Authorities found it nearly impossible to suppress ideas once they were mass-produced.

Furthermore, the printing press accelerated both the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution. Scholars could now rely on standardized, accurate texts, charts, and mathematical tables rather than error-prone manuscripts. By enabling researchers to share discoveries and build upon one another's work, the printing press created an enduring culture of shared knowledge that propelled Europe into the modern era.

There is an undeniable magic to San Francisco when the skies open up and a steady Pacific drizzle washes over the city’s famous hills. While sunshine shows off its postcard perfection, a rainy day reveals a moody, cinematic side that begs you to slow down and soak in the atmosphere. Grab a sturdy umbrella, as the bay breezes are notoriously unforgiving, and wander the slick, glistening streets where cable car bells echo softly through the mist. Along the waterfront, the Golden Gate Bridge plays a captivating game of hide and seek behind drifting clouds, making a fleeting glimpse of its orange towers feel like a rare gift. When the downpour intensifies, seek refuge inside the historic Ferry Building, where the rich aroma of roasted espresso and warm sourdough bread instantly revives your spirit. Later, stroll through Chinatown to watch vibrant red lanterns glow brilliantly against the gray afternoon, reflecting in puddles along Grant Avenue. You can duck into a North Beach café or an independent bookstore to wait out a passing squall. By twilight, neon signs shimmer across wet asphalt, turning steep avenues into rivers of color and proving that rain only deepens the timeless charm of this coastal gem.

San Francisco wears the rain like a velvet coat, transforming its steep streets into glistening mirrors that reflect the warm glow of corner cafes. When the Pacific storm clouds roll over the bay, the bustling crowds thin out, offering a rare and quiet intimacy with the city. Morning begins best inside a cozy North Beach bakery, where the scent of freshly baked sourdough and dark espresso fogs up the front windows while raindrops drum steadily against the glass. Armed with a sturdy umbrella, you can wander down into Chinatown, where vibrant red lanterns sway in the damp breeze and slick pavement captures glowing neon signs. A ride on a historic cable car feels especially nostalgic in a downpour, as the brass bell clangs through the thick mist and passengers huddle beneath the wooden roof to watch the skyline disappear into heavy fog. By afternoon, ducking into the Ferry Building provides a welcome shelter filled with artisan cheeses, flaky pastries, and steaming bowls of clam chowder. Watching the boats glide across the choppy water makes the chill worthwhile. Even without golden California sunshine, this moody atmosphere reveals a poetic charm across the hills that lingers long after your wet shoes dry.

Stepping into Kaze Ramen, the rich, savory aroma immediately promises an unforgettable meal. Unfortunately, your patience will be thoroughly tested before you take a single slurp.

The service here moves at a glacial pace. It took fifteen minutes just to receive menus, and another twenty before our orders were taken. Even water refills felt like a rare privilege. Despite the dining room being only half full, the staff seemed strangely unhurried and disorganized.

Yet, the moment the steaming bowl finally arrived, my frustration melted away. The tonkotsu broth is an absolute masterpiece. Simmered to perfection, it is velvety, deeply complex, and bursting with rich umami flavor that coats the palate without feeling overly heavy. Every spoonful tastes like hours of dedicated craft. While the noodles and chashu pork were solid, that liquid gold steals the show.

Come for the extraordinary broth, but do not arrive starving or in a rush.

Stepping into Golden Bowl Ramen, the rich aroma of simmering pork bones immediately promises an unforgettable meal. Unfortunately, you will have plenty of time to appreciate that scent before tasting anything. The service here is painfully slow. After waiting twenty minutes just to place our order, another forty minutes passed before the steaming bowls finally arrived at our table. Water glasses sat empty while the kitchen struggled to keep pace with a fairly quiet dining room.

Yet, one spoonful of the tonkotsu broth nearly erased my frustration. Velvety, deeply savory, and remarkably complex, it clearly reflects hours of patient simmering. The handmade noodles had a lovely chew, and the marinated egg was cooked to silky perfection, though the broth easily remained the undisputed star of the dish.

Visit Golden Bowl Ramen only when your schedule is completely open. The extraordinary broth justifies the patience, provided you arrive prepared to wait.

While remote work offers undeniable flexibility, it ultimately hurts junior engineers during the most critical phase of their professional development. Novice developers thrive on learning through osmosis, which happens naturally when sitting near senior colleagues, overhearing architectural debates, and absorbing quick debugging strategies. In a remote setting, this ambient mentorship largely disappears. Furthermore, digital communication creates friction that disproportionately affects beginners. An engineer in a physical office can easily gauge whether a teammate is available for a brief question with a simple glance. Online, however, every inquiry feels like a formal interruption requiring a message or a scheduled video call. This barrier often triggers imposter syndrome, causing juniors to struggle alone for hours out of fear of bothering busy teammates. Remote environments also slow down the trust and rapport building necessary for candid code reviews and psychological safety. Although distributed teams can mitigate these drawbacks through structured onboarding, dedicated pair programming, and frequent conversations, such practices demand consistent discipline that many growing companies struggle to maintain. Without the spontaneous collaboration and immediate feedback loops of a shared workspace, junior engineers face a steeper, lonelier climb toward technical autonomy, making fully remote setups a net disadvantage for new software engineering talent.

Remote work ultimately hurts junior engineers more than it helps them, despite the undeniable appeal of flexibility and eliminated commutes. For novice developers, the first couple of years in the industry are critical for absorbing unwritten norms, learning how to navigate complex codebases, and building professional intuition. In a physical office, junior engineers benefit immensely from ambient learning. They overhear architectural discussions, observe how senior developers debug tricky issues in real time, and can quickly tap a teammate on the shoulder for a brief explanation before getting stuck for hours. Remote environments replace these organic interactions with scheduled video calls and asynchronous messages, creating friction that often makes new hires hesitant to ask for help out of fear of seeming incompetent. Furthermore, building genuine mentorship and visibility is significantly harder through a computer screen. When promotions and major projects are handed out, managers naturally gravitate toward engineers they interact with frequently and trust deeply. While seasoned professionals with established networks thrive in remote setups, junior engineers risk isolation, slower skill acquisition, and stalled career momentum. Until companies master structured virtual onboarding and active mentorship, a traditional office or hybrid environment remains far superior for launching a successful software engineering career.

Running and swimming are two of the most effective cardiovascular exercises for staying fit, yet they offer distinctly different benefits and challenges.

Running is a weight-bearing, high-impact activity primarily targeting the lower body and core. Its biggest advantages are convenience and efficiency: all you need is a good pair of shoes and a route. Because you support your body weight against gravity, running typically burns slightly more calories per minute than moderate swimming and helps improve bone density. However, the repetitive impact on hard surfaces places stress on the knees, ankles, and hips, increasing the risk of overuse injuries.

Swimming, by contrast, is a low-impact, full-body workout. The natural resistance of water engages the arms, shoulders, back, core, and legs simultaneously, building balanced muscular endurance alongside cardiovascular health. Because water supports your body weight, swimming is remarkably gentle on the joints, making it ideal for people with arthritis, older adults, or athletes recovering from injuries. Its main drawbacks are accessibility and logistics, as it requires access to a pool or safe open water, plus extra time for changing and showering.

Ultimately, running excels for convenience, bone strength, and high calorie burn, while swimming shines for joint protection and total-body conditioning. Many fitness enthusiasts combine both for a well-rounded routine.

Running and swimming are both premier cardiovascular exercises, yet they offer distinct advantages and challenges for staying fit.

Running is a forceful activity that strengthens bones and builds endurance in the lower body. Because each stride absorbs ground impact, it burns calories rapidly and boosts bone density. However, that repetitive stress can strain the knees, ankles, and hips over time. Swimming offers the opposite experience. Water buoyancy supports your weight, creating an environment free of joint impact while still delivering an intense cardiovascular workout.

The two activities also differ in muscular engagement. Running primarily targets the legs, glutes, and core. Swimming provides balanced conditioning for the entire body, working the shoulders, back, arms, core, and legs simultaneously against water resistance.

Convenience is another key factor. Running requires only supportive shoes and an open path, making it accessible almost anywhere at any time. Swimming depends on pool availability, facility schedules, and extra gear, which can reduce spontaneity.

Ultimately, both sports build exceptional stamina and heart health. Running excels in convenience and bone strength, whereas swimming leads in joint protection and balanced muscle tone. Your ideal choice depends on your physical needs, daily routine, and personal enjoyment.

1/5 Unpopular opinion for junior devs: writing clever code is a trap.

Early in my career, I loved cryptic shortcuts and complex abstractions. Now I know better.

Here is why simple, boring code wins every single time.

2/5 Code is read far more often than it is written.

When production breaks at 2 AM, you do not want to decipher a clever puzzle. You want obvious, predictable logic that points straight to the bug.

Clarity saves sleep.

3/5 Software engineering is a team sport.

If only you can understand your function, it is a liability. Simple code lowers the cognitive load for your teammates and makes onboarding new developers effortless.

Write for humans first, computers second.

4/5 Requirements always change.

Clever code often relies on tight coupling and rigid tricks. When the business pivots, that cleverness turns into painful technical debt.

Simple code is easy to change and even easier to delete when you no longer need it.

5/5 True engineering mastery is not about showing off how smart you are.

Anyone can make a simple problem look complex. It takes real skill to make a complex problem look simple.

Aim for boring. Your future self will thank you.
